source_refs.note: Beta Decay: a main subheading of 12.4 Radioactivity, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 266-266.

blocks.text: There are two types of β-decay, beta-minus decay and beta-plus decay.

Some nuclides have neutron-to-proton ratio (N/P) too large and are the source of β⁻-decay. The β-particles are not the orbital electrons but they are created within the nucleus at the moment of emission. In this process, a neutron in the nucleus decays into a proton and an electron, plus another particle called antineutrino which is the anti-particle of neutrino. The neutrino is denoted by a Greek symbol ν (nu) and antineutrino is denoted by a bar over the ν̄. The decay process is given by the following relation:

One of the neutrons changes to a proton and in order to conserve charge it emits an electron. These electrons are called beta particles. However, they are indistinguishable from orbital electrons. Both the neutrino and the anti-neutrino have zero charge and very small mass, which is why they are very difficult to observe when passing through the matter. No nucleons are lost when a β-particle is emitted, and the total number of nucleons A remains the same but the mass number Z changes. Beta decay process can be written as:

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Z is the atomic number, not the mass number. In beta-minus decay the mass number A stays the same and the atomic number Z increases by one.

blocks.text_alt: ᴬ_Z X → ᴬ_(Z+1) X + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄

blocks.text: From the above equation, it is clear that the parent element of atomic number Z is transmuted to another element of atomic number (Z+1). An example is the isotope of thorium, which is unstable and decays into protactinium by beta emission. The reaction is represented as:

blocks.title: For Your Information
blocks.text: The neutrino was first proposed by Wolfgang Pauli in 1930 to obey the energy conservation in the beta-minus and beta-plus decays. Later in 1953, neutrino was detected by F. Reines and C. L. Cowan in a high-power nuclear reactor. On this discovery, F. Reines received the Nobel prize in 1995.

There are also nuclides that have neutron-to-proton ratio (N/P) too small for stability and decay by emitting a positron instead of an electron. The positron (e⁺) has the same mass as the electron but it has a positive charge. The positron is the antiparticle of the electron. In this process, a proton in the nucleus decays into a neutron and a positron, plus a neutrino. The generalized decay is given below:

blocks.text_alt: ᴬ_Z X → ᴬ_(Z−1) X + ⁰₊₁e + ν
